newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's missile killer intercepts target in test.
newsitem.headline: Israel's missile killer intercepts target in test.

text.p: Israel's Arrow 2 missile killer successfully intercepted a projectile over the Mediterranean in a test fire on Tuesday, officials said.
The Arrow's warhead failed to explode due to a system malfunction but it still managed to destroy the training missile.

"One of the sub-systems did not work properly and the warhead did not explode. Despite that we view the interception itself and the destruction of the target as a success," said Moshe Keret, director-general of Israel Aircraft Industries (IAI), the project's main contractor.
Tuesday's 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) launch was the fourth test for the Arrow 2. The missile, jointly financed by Israel and the United States, was last tested in August.
Security sources estimate the two countries have poured $500 million into the project since 1991. The projected cost is $1.6 billion but analysts say the missile could cost many times that figure.
Israel receives $1.8 billion in annual U.S. military grants. An agreement between the two countries gives the United States access to the Arrow's research and development data.
Keret said the missile would be operational by the end of 1998, 10 years after the programme began.
The Arrow started as part of the U.S. Strategic Defence Initiative, or "Star Wars", but took off on its own when Iraq fired dozens of Scud missiles at Israel in the 1991 Gulf War.
Iraqi missiles caused few casualties but the psychological effect on Israelis and the ineffectiveness of U.S. Patriot missiles in intercepting Scuds made missile defence a priority.

The Arrow's radar, developed by a subsidiary of IAI, is designed to track missiles and guide the Arrow at a speed of nearly three kms (two miles) per second to within four metres (13 ft) of an incoming missile.
The Arrow is supposed to intercept missiles between 10 km (six miles) and 40 km (25 miles) above the ground.
